analysis.one_liner: Bans corporations convicted of fraud felonies from funding election campaigns for ten years.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by one lawmaker with three cosponsors, sent to the House Administration Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar any corporation convicted of a fraud-related federal felony — or that paid $1 million or more to settle such charges through a deferred-prosecution or non-prosecution deal — from spending money on federal, state, or local election campaigns for ten years. That ban would cover direct contributions, independent expenditures, and issue ads, including spending through corporate political action funds. It would only apply to corporations convicted or settling after the bill's enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters and candidates running against corporate-backed money: companies found to have committed fraud against the government or the public would lose their ability to flood campaigns with cash for a decade. The bill also sends a signal that a criminal conviction carries a real political consequence. Ordinary people who currently face campaign spending from companies that have pleaded guilty to or settled felony charges would gain a measure of protection from that money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters seeking to curb corporate campaign money

how_it_helps.text: It makes political spending unlawful for ten years for any corporation finally convicted of conspiracy to defraud the United States or any other felony involving dishonesty or breach of trust.

It closes the plea-deal loophole: a corporation that avoids conviction by signing a deferred-prosecution or non-prosecution agreement with a payment of $1 million or more is treated the same as a convicted company.

The ban covers every form of campaign money the law allows corporations to spend — contributions, independent expenditures, and electioneering communications — and applies to federal, state, and local elections alike, including through corporate PACs.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations with felony fraud convictions or large settlement agreements would lose their ability to spend on elections for ten years, including through their political action committees. No public funds are spent. The broader cost falls on large companies exposed to federal criminal charges, and arguably on the political committees and candidates that currently receive their money.

drawbacks.text: The ban only applies going forward: a company already convicted of fraud, or already under a settlement agreement, when the bill passes would face no restriction, so the best-known cases of corporate offenders would be untouched.

The reach is narrow — it only captures corporations with federal criminal convictions or qualifying settlement deals, not companies that pay civil fines or settle with other agencies for the same misconduct, so much corporate spending from companies accused of wrongdoing would remain legal.

Restricting corporate political spending based on criminal status would likely face a First Amendment court challenge, since the Supreme Court's Citizens United line of decisions has generally protected corporate independent spending; the bill could be struck down or narrowed in litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea — that a company found guilty of defrauding the United States should not then spend money to influence elections — has real public value and costs taxpayers nothing. But the design is narrow: it exempts existing offenders, relies on federal convictions that are rare for large companies, and would almost certainly be tested in court. As drafted it is more a statement of principle than a sweeping fix for corporate money in politics.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Administration Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing or vote until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced the bill on May 23, 2024, joined by three Democratic cosponsors: Reps. Jan Schakowsky, Rashida Tlaib, and Ayanna Pressley.
The House referred it to the Committee on House Administration the same day, and no further action of any kind was taken for the rest of the 118th Congress.
No committee hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate companion action appears in the record, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations with criminal convictions or large fraud settlements keep their full rights to spend on elections, and the status quo of corporate campaign money is untouched. No member of Congress had to take a public position on the bill because it never came to a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporate offenders and the campaign-money status quo

for.name: Rep. Ilhan Omar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought a ban on campaign spending by convicted corporations.

for.name: Reps. Jan Schakowsky, Rashida Tlaib, and Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; the only three cosponsors it ever drew.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no report.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; the only evidence is that all four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support at any point.

industries.industry: Large corporations with criminal convictions or federal fraud settlements
industries.note: These companies would lose the ability to fund candidates, run political ads, or operate political action funds for ten years after a felony fraud conviction or a $1 million-plus settlement deal. Their interest in preserving unlimited political spending runs directly against the bill's aim of keeping fraud-tainted money out of elections.

industries.industry: Political consulting and campaign advertising firms
industries.note: A source of large corporate clients would be curtailed whenever a major company is convicted or settles fraud charges, shrinking demand for campaign services from those firms. The effect is limited because the bill applies only prospectively and to a small set of companies.
